transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Korova Coleman, Ukraine resumed attacks on Russian
energy sites overnight.
The move follows signals by Ukraine it would no longer abide by an energy cease-fire declared
by President Trump.
From Moscow, NPR's Charles Maines has details.
Ukrainian drones set fire to a key oil refinery that services Moscow.
The local authorities said the scale of the damage was unclear.
The strike came just hours after President Vladimir Zelensky declared an end to a self-imposed
three-day pause on attacks on Russia's oil infrastructure, citing the Kremlin's own refusal
to abide by the Trump energy cease-fire.
That Trump proposal, however, has come with added pressure on Ukraine to stop its targeting
of Russian oil or lose access to American military intelligence.
In recent days, Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukraine's strikes on Russia's gas industry
rather than the war in Iran for driving up fuel costs in the U.S. ahead of midterm elections.
Charles Maines, NPR News, Moscow.
Saudi Arabia has issued alerts across the southern parts of its country near Yemen.
That's after Houthi rebels in Yemen fired at the headquarters of the Saudi oil company
Aramco.
NPR's Aya Batrawi reports this comes days after the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia
in more than a decade.
The Houthis who are backed by Iran say they were striking Aramco's offices in response
to Saudi jets bombing an oil facility in Yemen's capital of Sana'a and other fuel sites Tuesday.
And the Houthis and Saudis both say they struck each other's oil sites because they're used
to support military operations.
The Saudis are carrying out a major offensive with Yemeni government forces against the Houthis.
And the Houthis say Saudi Arabia has launched more than 2,000 airstrikes on Yemen in past
weeks killing civilians.
And Biers Aya Batrawi reporting.
Another Venezuelan leader, Nicolas Maduro, and his wife, Celia Flores, are scheduled
to return to federal court today in New York City.
They will face additional charges of torturing political opponents.
U.S. forces took the couple from Venezuela in early January.
They came to face drug and weapons counts in the United States.
The couple are scheduled to go on trial next June.
When the Faculty Senate at Cornell University met yesterday, they've started a no-confidence
process on university leadership.
And Piers Alyssa Nadwani prepared this report.
University President Michael Kotlikoff joined the faculty meeting to take questions and
talk about what the school is doing to address safety on campus.
But faculty still went ahead on beginning a no-confidence vote, which is expected in
a few weeks.
It's an opportunity to voice their dissatisfaction with the administration, but ultimately, Kotlikoff's
job will be in the hands of the Board of Trustees, a group that includes donors and alumni.
They'll be meeting on campus starting Thursday.
Alyssa Nadwani, NPR News Ithaca, New York.
This is NPR.
Weather forecasters say dangerous Santa Ana winds are returning to northern California.
These can trigger wildfires, and in the past, some fires have been deadly and destructive.
The National Weather Service has posted red flag warnings for much of California today.
The service is cautioning high winds and very dry conditions can help trigger new fires.
The Vatican says that Pope Leo has spent a good second night at a hospital in Rome.
Leo had surgery two days ago.
This removed the lower part of his right lung to address cancer.
The Vatican says that Leo is eating, he is up and walking, and his condition is progressing
normally.
Scientists say elephants have an outsized effect on landscapes both in life and in death.
And Piers Alana Gordon reports.
Elephants are ecosystem engineers.
They knock down trees, they disperse seeds, but scientists in South Africa's Kruger National
Park found something they didn't expect after the animals die.
The group monitored dozens of elephant carcasses on the savannah, and found that over time,
the remains created unique, nutrient-rich hotspots for certain grasses.
This drew animals like zebras and antelope well after any visual signs of the elephant
had disappeared.
Courtney Reed is with UC Santa Barbara in Princeton.
She led the research.
Seeing that even like eight years on, you have all of these different herbivores that live
on the savannah that are really selecting for those nitrogen-rich grasses.
It was just exciting.
Reed says this lasting legacy highlights the importance of elephants as they face threats
of extinction.
The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Alana Gordon, NPR News.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian energy sites, drone strike sets Moscow-serving refinery ablaze
Saudi Arabia issues alerts in southern regions after Houthi fire at Aramco headquarters
Maduro and wife Celia Flores return to New York federal court on new torture charges
Cornell Faculty Senate begins no-confidence process against President Michael Kotlikoff
Dangerous Santa Ana winds return to northern California, red flag warnings posted
Pope Leo recovering normally at Rome hospital after lung cancer surgery
Study finds elephant carcasses create lasting nutrient-rich grass hotspots in Kruger National Park
